Appendix A Lattice periodicity

In this appendix, we discuss the details of the DFPT formalism for periodic solids. In particular, we show how linear-response quantities in a supercell with an isolated perturbation (i.e. a perturbation that has the periodicity of the supercell) can be rewritten as a sum of monochromatic 𝐪\mathbf{q} components in a primitive unit cell.

A.1 Bloch sums of localized functions and Bloch functions

We start from setting the formalism of Bloch sums and their lattice-periodic parts.

Using the fact that I=(l,s)I=(l,s), with ll being the cell index (𝐑l\mathbf{R}_{l} pointing to the cell), and ss being the atomic index (𝝉s\bm{\tau}_{s} inside cell 𝐑l\mathbf{R}_{l}), so that the position of atom II is 𝐑l+𝝉s\mathbf{R}_{l}+\bm{\tau}_{s}, we have that the localized functions are

φmI​(𝐫)=φml,s​(𝐫)=φms​(𝐫−𝐑l)=φmγ⁡(s)​(𝐫−𝐑l−𝝉s),\varphi^{I}_{m}(\mathbf{r})=\varphi^{l,s}_{m}(\mathbf{r})=\varphi^{s}_{m}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{l})=\varphi^{\gamma(s)}_{m}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{l}-\bm{\tau}_{s})\,, (50)

where γ⁡(s)\gamma(s) is the atomic type of the ss-th atom. In a periodic solid, we can construct Bloch sums of localized functions (50) [84]. By doing so we obtain:

φ~m,𝐤s​(𝐫)=1N𝐤​∑𝐑lN𝐤ei​𝐤⋅𝐑l​φms​(𝐫−𝐑l),\tilde{\varphi}^{s}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\mathbf{k}}}}\sum_{\mathbf{R}_{l}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l}}\,\varphi^{s}_{m}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{l})\,, (51)

where summations run over the N𝐤N_{\mathbf{k}} primitive unit cells of the Born-von Karman supercell. Given Eq. (51), we can define inverse Bloch sums as

φms(𝐫−𝐑l)=1N𝐤∑𝐤N𝐤e−i𝐤⋅𝐑lφ~m,𝐤s(𝐫).\varphi^{s}_{m}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{l})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\mathbf{k}}}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l}}\,\tilde{\varphi}^{s}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\,. (52)

It is useful to recall the analogy of Eqs. (51) and (52) with those between KS wave functions and Wannier functions (see e.g. Ref. [85]).

According to Bloch theorem, in periodic solids the ground-state KS wave functions can be written as:

ψv​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)=1N𝐤​ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​u¯v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫),\psi_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\mathbf{k}}}}\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,, (53)

where u¯v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}) are the lattice-periodic parts of the ground-state KS wave functions [u¯v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫+𝐑l)=u¯v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{R}_{l})=\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})]. The functions φ~m,𝐤s​(𝐫)\tilde{\varphi}^{s}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) are Bloch-like functions, as ψv​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\psi_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}), and can also be expressed in the same way:

φ~m,𝐤s​(𝐫)=1N𝐤​ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​φ¯m,𝐤s​(𝐫),\tilde{\varphi}^{s}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\mathbf{k}}}}\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\bar{\varphi}^{s}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\,, (54)

where φ¯m,𝐤s​(𝐫)\bar{\varphi}^{s}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) is defined as

φ¯m,𝐤s(𝐫)≡e−i𝐤⋅𝝉sφ¯m,𝐤γ⁡(s)(𝐫−𝝉s).\bar{\varphi}^{s}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\equiv e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\bm{\tau}_{s}}\,\bar{\varphi}^{\gamma(s)}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}-\bm{\tau}_{s})\,. (55)

The normalization factor 1/N𝐤1/\sqrt{N_{\mathbf{k}}} has been chosen such that the lattice-periodic functions u¯v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}) are normalized to unity in the primitive unit cell, with inner products involving them understood as integrals over one primitive unit cell, namely:

⟨ψv​𝐤​σ|ψv′​𝐤′​σ′⟩\displaystyle\langle\psi_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}|\psi_{v^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle ≡\displaystyle\equiv ∫Vψv​𝐤​σ∗​(𝐫)​ψv′​𝐤′​σ′​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫\displaystyle\int\limits_{\mathrm{V}}\psi^{*}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,\psi_{v^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r} (56)
=\displaystyle= δ𝐤,𝐤′​⟨u¯v​𝐤​σ|u¯v′​𝐤​σ′⟩,\displaystyle\delta_{\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}\,\langle\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}|\bar{u}_{v^{\prime}\mathbf{k}\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle\,,

where

⟨u¯v​𝐤​σ|u¯v′​𝐤​σ′⟩\displaystyle\langle\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}|\bar{u}_{v^{\prime}\mathbf{k}\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle ≡\displaystyle\equiv ∫vu¯v​𝐤​σ∗​(𝐫)​u¯v′​𝐤​σ′​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫\displaystyle\int\limits_{\mathrm{v}}\bar{u}^{*}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,\bar{u}_{v^{\prime}\mathbf{k}\sigma^{\prime}}(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r} (57)
=\displaystyle= δv​v′​δσ​σ′,\displaystyle\delta_{vv^{\prime}}\delta_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\,,

where v\mathrm{v} is the volume of the primitive unit cell and V=v​N𝐤\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{v}\,N_{\mathbf{k}}. Here we use the notation ⟨a|b⟩\langle a|b\rangle which stands for the inner product between aa and bb over the whole crystal of volume V\mathrm{V} when aa and bb represent ψv​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\psi_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}), and the inner product over the primitive unit cell of volume v\mathrm{v} when aa and bb represent u¯v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}).

A.2 Ground state quantities

In this section, we will show how to rewrite all ground-state quantities that enter DFPT (see Sec. IV.1) as the product of a lattice-periodic part and appropriate phase factors. The derivation is based on the equations of Sec. A.1.

Using Eqs. (11) and (53) it is easy to show that the ground-state spin charge density can be written as:

ρσ∘​(𝐫)=1N𝐤​∑𝐤N𝐤∑vNocc|u¯v​𝐤​σ∘​(𝐫)|2.\rho^{\circ}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{v}^{N_{\mathrm{occ}}}|\bar{u}^{\circ}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})|^{2}\,. (58)

Similarly, it can be shown that using Eqs. (3), (4), (52), (53), and (54), the ground-state occupation matrices can be written as:

nm1​m2s​σ=1N𝐤​∑𝐤N𝐤∑vNocc⟨u¯v​𝐤​σ∘|P¯^m2,m1,𝐤,𝐤s|u¯v​𝐤​σ∘⟩,n_{m_{1}m_{2}}^{s\sigma}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{v}^{N_{\mathrm{occ}}}\langle\bar{u}^{\circ}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}|\hat{\bar{P}}^{s}_{m_{2},m_{1},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}}|\bar{u}^{\circ}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}\rangle\,, (59)

where P¯^m2,m1,𝐤,𝐤s\hat{\bar{P}}^{s}_{m_{2},m_{1},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}} corresponds to the 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}={\bf 0} case of Eq. (44). It is important to stress that the ground-state occupation matrices (59) do not depend on the index of the primitive unit cell, which is a consequence of the periodicity of the crystal.

The ground state Hamiltonian, Eq. (6), in the coordinate representation can be represented as:

Hσ∘(𝐫,𝐫′)=1N𝐤∑𝐤N𝐤ei​𝐤⋅𝐫H¯𝐤,σ∘(𝐫,𝐫′)e−i𝐤⋅𝐫′,H^{\circ}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\bar{H}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r^{\prime}})\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}\,, (60)

where the Bloch phases and the lattice-periodic part have been separated and the latter reads:

H¯𝐤,σ∘​(𝐫,𝐫′)=H¯DFT,𝐤,σ∘​(𝐫,𝐫′)+V¯Hub,𝐤,σ∘​(𝐫,𝐫′),\bar{H}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r^{\prime}})=\bar{H}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{DFT},\mathbf{k},\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r^{\prime}})+\bar{V}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Hub},\mathbf{k},\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r^{\prime}})\,, (61)

which in the operator form can be written as:

H¯^𝐤,σ∘=H¯^DFT,𝐤,σ∘+V¯^Hub,𝐤,σ∘.\hat{\bar{H}}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}=\hat{\bar{H}}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{DFT},\mathbf{k},\sigma}+\hat{\bar{V}}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Hub},\mathbf{k},\sigma}\,. (62)

The first term in Eq. (62) can be expressed as:

H¯^DFT,𝐤,σ∘=−12​(∇+i​𝐤)2+V¯^NL,𝐤∘+V^loc∘+V^Hxc∘,\hat{\bar{H}}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{DFT},\mathbf{k},\sigma}=-\frac{1}{2}(\nabla+i\mathbf{k})^{2}+\hat{\bar{V}}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{NL},\mathbf{k}}+\hat{V}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{loc}}+\hat{V}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Hxc}}\,, (63)

where the first term is the kinetic energy operator, V¯^NL,𝐤∘\hat{\bar{V}}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{NL},\mathbf{k}} is the lattice-periodic component of the non-local part of PP as in standard DFT plane-wave implementations [47, 69], and the last two terms are the local part of PP and Hxc potentials. The non-locality of H¯DFT,𝐤,σ∘​(𝐫,𝐫′)\bar{H}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{DFT},\mathbf{k},\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r^{\prime}}) comes from the non-locality of V¯NL,𝐤∘​(𝐫,𝐫′)\bar{V}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{NL},\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}). VHxc∘​(𝐫)V^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Hxc}}(\mathbf{r}) is defined in Eqs. (9) and (10), using the expression for the ground-state spin charge density (58). The lattice-periodic part of the ground-state Hubbard potential, i.e. second term in Eq. (62), reads [see Eq. (8)]:

V¯^Hub,𝐤,σ∘=∑s​m1​m2Us​(δm1​m22−nm1​m2s​σ)​P¯^m1,m2,𝐤,𝐤s,\hat{\bar{V}}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Hub},\mathbf{k},\sigma}=\sum_{sm_{1}m_{2}}U^{s}\left(\frac{\delta_{m_{1}m_{2}}}{2}-n^{s\,\sigma}_{m_{1}m_{2}}\right)\hat{\bar{P}}^{s}_{m_{1},m_{2},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}}\,, (64)

where nm1​m2s​σn^{s\,\sigma}_{m_{1}m_{2}} is given by Eq. (59), and P¯^m1,m2,𝐤,𝐤s\hat{\bar{P}}^{s}_{m_{1},m_{2},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}} can be obtained from Eq. (44) by taking 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0}. As was noted for the ground-state occupation matrices [see Eq. (59)], also V¯^Hub,𝐤,σ∘\hat{\bar{V}}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Hub},\mathbf{k},\sigma} does not depend on the index of the primitive unit cell due to the periodicity of the crystal.

Finally, let us consider the projectors on occupied and empty states, 𝒪^σ\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{\sigma} and 𝒫^σ\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\sigma}, which appear in Eq. (27). Similarly to Eq. (60), the operator 𝒪^σ\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{\sigma} can be written in the coordinate representation as:

𝒪σ(𝐫,𝐫′)=1N𝐤∑𝐤′N𝐤ei​𝐤′⋅𝐫𝒪¯𝐤′​σ(𝐫,𝐫′)e−i𝐤′⋅𝐫′,\mathcal{O}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{i\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}\,, (65)

where 𝒪¯𝐤′​σ​(𝐫,𝐫′)\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) is the lattice-periodic part defined as:

𝒪¯𝐤′​σ​(𝐫,𝐫′)=∑vNoccu¯v​𝐤′​σ∘​(𝐫)​u¯v​𝐤′​σ∘⁣∗​(𝐫′).\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\sum_{v}^{N_{\mathrm{occ}}}\bar{u}^{\circ}_{v\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,\bar{u}^{\circ\,*}_{v\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,. (66)

Using an operator notation it is possible to express the same projector as follows:

𝒪¯^𝐤′​σ=∑v′Nocc|u¯v′​𝐤′​σ∘⟩​⟨u¯v′​𝐤′​σ∘|.\hat{\bar{\mathcal{O}}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}=\sum_{v^{\prime}}^{N_{\mathrm{occ}}}|\bar{u}^{\circ}_{v^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}\rangle\langle\bar{u}^{\circ}_{v^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}|\,. (67)

In the same manner it can be shown that the operator 𝒫^σ\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\sigma} can be written in the coordinate representation as:

𝒫σ(𝐫,𝐫′)=1N𝐤∑𝐤′N𝐤ei​𝐤′⋅𝐫𝒫¯𝐤′​σ(𝐫,𝐫′)e−i𝐤′⋅𝐫′,\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{i\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\bar{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}\,, (68)

where the lattice-periodic part 𝒫¯𝐤′​σ​(𝐫,𝐫′)\bar{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) can obviously be written as follows:

𝒫¯𝐤′​σ​(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= δ⁡(𝐫−𝐫′)−𝒪¯𝐤′​σ​(𝐫,𝐫′),\displaystyle\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})-\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,, (69)

which translates in the operator notation as:

𝒫¯^𝐤′​σ=1−𝒪¯^𝐤′​σ.\hat{\bar{\mathcal{P}}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}=1-\hat{\bar{\mathcal{O}}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\sigma}\,. (70)

A.3 Decomposition of linear-response quantities into monochromatic components

In this section, we will demonstrate how a localized, neutral perturbation that has the periodicity of a supercell (chosen large enough to mimic a truly isolated perturbation) can be recast as a sum of monochromatic (𝐪\mathbf{q}-specific) perturbations in a primitive unit cell, as discussed in Sec. IV.2.1. Let us start from the perturbing potential, Eq. (18). In periodic-boundary conditions perturbations cannot be isolated. In order to model the response of occupations to an isolated perturbation supercells must be used, whose size is chosen large enough to make interactions between periodic replicas negligible. In mathematical terms, this translates into the following approximation for the perturbing potential [Eq. (18)]:

Vperts′​l′​(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle V^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= ∑mφms′(𝐫−𝐑l′)φms′∗(𝐫−𝐑l′)\displaystyle\sum_{m}\varphi^{s^{\prime}}_{m}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}})\,\varphi^{s^{\prime}*}_{m}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}) (71)
≃\displaystyle\simeq ∑𝐑sc∑mφms′​(𝐫−𝐑l′−𝐑sc)\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}}\sum_{m}\varphi^{s^{\prime}}_{m}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}-\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}})
×φms′∗(𝐫−𝐑l′−𝐑sc).\displaystyle\hskip 22.76228pt\times\,\varphi^{s^{\prime}*}_{m}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}-\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}})\,.

If we approximate each of the localized functions in Eq. (71) with the inverse Bloch sums, Eq. (52), then the largest (nontrivial) supercell vectors 𝐑scmax\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}^{\mathrm{max}} on which the external sum in Eq. (71) runs over are such that 𝐑scmax⋅Δ​𝐤=2​π\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}^{\mathrm{max}}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{k}=2\pi, where Δ​𝐤\Delta\mathbf{k} is the minimum spacing between 𝐤\mathbf{k} points in the first Brillouin zone of the primitive unit cell. Larger 𝐑sc\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}’s are, in fact, implicitly summed over, because of the periodicity of inverse Bloch sums [see Eq. (52)]. Therefore, the external summation in Eq. (71) runs over NscN_{\mathrm{sc}} vectors 𝐑sc\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}, where Nsc=N𝐤sc=N𝐤/N𝐪N_{\mathrm{sc}}=N_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{sc}}=N_{\mathbf{k}}/N_{\mathbf{q}}. Thus, using Eq. (52) we can rewrite Eq. (71) as follows:

Vperts′​l′​(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle V^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= 1N𝐤∑𝐑scNsc∑m∑𝐤′N𝐤e−i𝐤′⋅𝐑l′φ~m,𝐤′s′(𝐫)\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}\sum_{m}\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{-i\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\,\tilde{\varphi}^{s^{\prime}}_{m,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{r}) (72)
×∑𝐤N𝐤ei​𝐤⋅𝐑l′φ~m,𝐤s′∗(𝐫)e−i(𝐤′−𝐤)⋅𝐑sc.\displaystyle\hskip-14.22636pt\times\,\sum_{\mathbf{k}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\,\tilde{\varphi}^{s^{\prime}*}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\,e^{-i(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k})\cdot\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}}\,.

In Eq. (72) the sum over 𝐑sc\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}} of the phase factor e−i(𝐤′−𝐤)⋅𝐑sce^{-i(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k})\cdot\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}} imposes the difference between 𝐤′\mathbf{k}^{\prime} and 𝐤\mathbf{k} to be equal to reciprocal lattice vectors of the supercell, which we label as 𝐪\mathbf{q} (see Sec. IV.2.1). Therefore, in the summation over 𝐤′\mathbf{k}^{\prime} only N𝐪N_{\mathbf{q}} terms survive, which correspond to 𝐤′=𝐤+𝐪\mathbf{k}^{\prime}=\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}. Thus, we obtain:

Vperts′​l′​(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle V^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= 1N𝐤∑𝐑scNsc∑m∑𝐪N𝐪∑𝐤N𝐤e−i(𝐤+𝐪)⋅𝐑l′φ~m,𝐤+𝐪s′(𝐫)\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}}^{N_{\mathrm{sc}}}\sum_{m}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}^{N_{\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{-i(\mathbf{k+q})\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\,\tilde{\varphi}^{s^{\prime}}_{m,\mathbf{k+q}}(\mathbf{r}) (73)
×ei​𝐤⋅𝐑l′φ~m,𝐤s′∗(𝐫)e−i𝐪⋅𝐑sc.\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\times\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\,\tilde{\varphi}^{s^{\prime}*}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\,e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}}\,.

Since 𝐪\mathbf{q} vectors are the reciprocal lattice vectors of the supercell, e−i𝐪⋅𝐑sc=1e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}}}=1, and the summation over 𝐑sc\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{sc}} gives a prefactor NscN_{\mathrm{sc}}. Equation (73) can thus be written as:

Vperts′​l′(𝐫,𝐫′)=1N𝐪∑𝐪N𝐪e−i𝐪⋅𝐑l′∑m∑𝐤N𝐤φ~m,𝐤+𝐪s′(𝐫)φ~m,𝐤s′∗(𝐫).V^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}^{N_{\mathbf{q}}}e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\sum_{m}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\tilde{\varphi}^{s^{\prime}}_{m,\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{r})\,\tilde{\varphi}^{s^{\prime}*}_{m,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\,. (74)

Finally, by using Eq. (54), we can rewrite Eq. (74) as:

Vperts′​l′(𝐫,𝐫′)=1N𝐪∑𝐪N𝐪e−i𝐪⋅𝐑l′Vpert,𝐪s′(𝐫,𝐫′),V^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}^{N_{\mathbf{q}}}e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\,V^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert},\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,, (75)

where

Vpert,𝐪s′(𝐫,𝐫′)=1N𝐤∑𝐤N𝐤ei⁡(𝐤+𝐪)⋅𝐫V¯pert,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤s′(𝐫,𝐫′)e−i𝐤⋅𝐫′.V^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert},\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{k}}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}^{N_{\mathbf{k}}}e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\bar{V}^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert},\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}\,. (76)

In Eq. (76), V¯pert,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤s′​(𝐫,𝐫′)\bar{V}^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert},\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) is the lattice-periodic part of the perturbing potential:

V¯pert,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤s′​(𝐫,𝐫′)=∑mP¯m,m,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤s′​(𝐫,𝐫′),\bar{V}^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert},\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\sum_{m}\bar{P}^{s^{\prime}}_{m,m,\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,, (77)

with P¯m,m,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤s′​(𝐫,𝐫′)\bar{P}^{s^{\prime}}_{m,m,\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) representing the diagonal element of the lattice-periodic operator in the coordinate representation which reads:

P¯m2,m1,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤s(𝐫,𝐫′)=φ¯m2,𝐤+𝐪s(𝐫)φ¯m1,𝐤s∗(𝐫′).\bar{P}^{s}_{m_{2},m_{1},\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\bar{\varphi}^{s}_{m_{2},\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{r})\,\bar{\varphi}^{s*}_{m_{1},\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,. (78)

Equation (78) can be written in operator form [see Eq. (44)]. Equation (75) constitutes a decomposition of the isolated perturbing potential into monochromatic components modulated by a phase factor corresponding to the considered wave vector 𝐪\mathbf{q} [86].

Similarly to the decomposition of the perturbing potential, Eq. (75), we can represent the LR KS wave functions of the supercell as the inverse Bloch sum of the LR KS wave functions of the primitive unit cell:

d​ψ~v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)d​λs′​l′=1N𝐪∑𝐪N𝐪e−i𝐪⋅𝐑l′Δ𝐪s′ψ~v​𝐤​σ(𝐫),\frac{d\tilde{\psi}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})}{d\lambda^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}^{N_{\mathbf{q}}}e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\,\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{\psi}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,, (79)

where Δ𝐪s′​ψ~v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{\psi}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}) are the LR KS wave functions of the primitive unit cell corresponding to the monochromatic perturbation with wave vector 𝐪\mathbf{q}, Vpert,𝐪s′V^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pert},\mathbf{q}}. From  (79) we can define the Bloch sum

Δ𝐪s′​ψ~v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)=∑𝐑l′N𝐪ei​𝐪⋅𝐑l′​d​ψ~v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)d​λs′​l′.\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{\psi}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}^{N_{\mathbf{q}}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\,\frac{d\tilde{\psi}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})}{d\lambda^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}}\,. (80)

It is important to note that the normalization factors 1/N𝐪1/N_{\mathbf{q}} in Eq. (79) and 1 in Eq. (80) are chosen in such a way that these definitions are consistent with the normalization in Eq. (75). The LR KS wave functions Δ𝐪s′​ψ~v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{\psi}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}) are Bloch-like functions, and hence they can be written as:

Δ𝐪s′​ψ~v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)=1N𝐤​ei⁡(𝐤+𝐪)⋅𝐫​Δ𝐪s′​u¯v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫),\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{\psi}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\mathbf{k}}}}\,e^{i(\mathbf{k+q})\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,, (81)

where Δ𝐪s′​u¯v​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\bar{u}_{v\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}) are the lattice-periodic functions, in agreement with the definition in Eq. (53).

Similarly to the decomposition of the perturbing potential and of the LR KS wave functions into monochromatic 𝐪\mathbf{q} components [see Eqs. (75) and (79), respectively], also the LR spin charge density can be decomposed into 𝐪\mathbf{q}-specific terms:

d​ρσ​(𝐫)d​λs′​l′=1N𝐪∑𝐪N𝐪e−i𝐪⋅𝐑l′Δ𝐪s′ρ~σ(𝐫),\frac{d\rho_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r})}{d\lambda^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}^{N_{\mathbf{q}}}e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{\rho}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,, (82)

where

Δ𝐪s′​ρ~σ​(𝐫)=ei​𝐪⋅𝐫​Δ𝐪s′​ρ¯σ​(𝐫),\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{\rho}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r})=e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\bar{\rho}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,, (83)

and Δ𝐪s′​ρ¯σ​(𝐫)\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\bar{\rho}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r}) is given by Eq. (48). Since the LR Hxc potential depends linearly on the variation in the spin charge density [see Eq. (24)], the decomposition in Eq. (82) means that also the LR Hxc potential can be decomposed in a similar way:

d​VHxc,σ​(𝐫)d​λs′​l′=1N𝐪∑𝐪N𝐪e−i𝐪⋅𝐑l′Δ𝐪s′V~Hxc,σ(𝐫),\frac{dV_{\mathrm{Hxc},\sigma}(\mathbf{r})}{d\lambda^{s^{\prime}l^{\prime}}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}^{N_{\mathbf{q}}}e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}}}\,\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{V}_{\mathrm{Hxc},\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,, (84)

where

Δ𝐪s′​V~Hxc,σ​(𝐫)=ei​𝐪⋅𝐫​Δ𝐪s′​V¯Hxc,σ​(𝐫),\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\tilde{V}_{\mathrm{Hxc},\sigma}(\mathbf{r})=e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\bar{V}_{\mathrm{Hxc},\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,, (85)

with Δ𝐪s′​V¯Hxc,σ​(𝐫)\Delta^{s^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{q}}\bar{V}_{\mathrm{Hxc},\sigma}(\mathbf{r}) given by Eq. (47).
